stem: What objective does standard k-means minimize?

options.A: The within-cluster sum of squared Euclidean distances from observations to their assigned cluster centroids (inertia).
options.B: Cross-entropy between predicted classes and labels.
options.C: The determinant of the covariance matrix of the whole dataset.

rationales.correct: K-means alternates between assigning points to the nearest centroid and recomputing centroids, decreasing the sum of squared within-cluster distances toward a local optimum.
rationales.B: K-means is unsupervised and does not require labels.
rationales.C: That is not the standard k-means objective.
rationales.D: Hidden labels are unavailable to the standard algorithm.

stem: Why can k-means produce different solutions on the same dataset when initialized differently?

options.A: Its iterative coordinate-descent-like procedure can converge to different local minima of the non-convex clustering objective.
options.B: The squared-distance objective is strictly concave.
options.C: Centroids are selected deterministically by class labels.

rationales.correct: The k-means objective is not convex jointly over assignments and centroids, so different starting centroids can lead to different local optima. Multiple initializations are used to mitigate this.
rationales.B: The objective is not strictly concave.
rationales.C: Standard k-means does not use labels.
rationales.D: Initialization can materially affect the result.

stem: Why is standard k-means a poor default for clusters that are strongly non-spherical and connected in curved shapes such as concentric rings?

options.A: Its centroid-and-Euclidean-distance objective favors compact Voronoi-like partitions rather than arbitrary curved connectivity.
options.B: K-means can only process categorical variables.

rationales.correct: Euclidean distance to a centroid works well for roughly compact, similarly shaped groups. Curved manifolds often require a different similarity or clustering formulation.
rationales.B: Categorical-only is not the issue; standard k-means is numeric and distance-based.

stem: An anomaly-detection feature is highly skewed and varies over orders of magnitude. Why might a log transform improve a distance-based clustering workflow?

options.A: It can compress extreme scale differences and reduce the dominance of very large values, depending on the data-generating process.
options.B: It guarantees Gaussianity in every dataset.
options.D: It makes Euclidean distance independent of feature scaling.

rationales.correct: A logarithm can compress multiplicative scale and reduce skew for positive-valued variables. It does not guarantee a particular distribution or remove all outliers.
rationales.B: Transformations can improve symmetry but do not guarantee normality.
rationales.D: Distances remain sensitive to the transformed feature scales.

stem: What is the silhouette coefficient trying to capture for a clustering assignment?

options.A: How similar a sample is to its own cluster compared with the nearest alternative cluster, balancing cohesion and separation.
options.C: The probability that every cluster has equal size.
options.D: The number of principal components in the dataset.

rationales.correct: Silhouette compares within-cluster dissimilarity with the nearest-cluster dissimilarity, producing values that are higher when points are cohesive to their assigned cluster and separated from alternatives.
rationales.B: It is an internal clustering criterion, not classification accuracy.

stem: A classifier outputs high confidence probabilities but is systematically overconfident. Which post-training technique is specifically designed to improve probability calibration?

options.A: Temperature scaling or another calibrated probability mapping fitted on held-out validation data.
options.C: Increasing the classification threshold to 0.99 for every application.
options.D: Replacing all probabilities with the argmax class index.

rationales.correct: Calibration methods learn a mapping from model scores to probabilities using held-out data. Temperature scaling is a common post-hoc method for neural classifiers.
rationales.C: A threshold changes decisions, not the underlying calibration curve.
rationales.D: Hard class indices discard probability information.

stem: Why can perplexity or likelihood-based criteria and clustering silhouette scores tell you different things about a model or representation?

options.A: They optimize different notions of fit: probabilistic criteria evaluate probability assignments under a model, while silhouette evaluates geometric cohesion/separation of clusters.
options.B: They are mathematically identical metrics with different names.
options.C: Silhouette is computed from class labels in all cases.
options.D: Likelihood can only be used for supervised learning.

rationales.correct: Different evaluation criteria encode different assumptions and goals. A representation can have good geometric separation yet fit a probabilistic model poorly, or vice versa.
rationales.C: Silhouette is usually an internal metric and can be computed without labels.
rationales.D: Likelihood is central to many unsupervised probabilistic models.

stem: A clustering result has a lower within-cluster SSE when k increases from 4 to 8. Why does this alone not prove k=8 is the better model?

options.A: The k-means objective is non-increasing as more clusters are allowed, so lower SSE alone rewards additional complexity and needs a model-selection or domain criterion.
options.B: Lower SSE is mathematically impossible when k increases.
options.D: A larger k automatically means more underfitting.

rationales.correct: With more centroids, points have more opportunities to be close to a centroid, so inertia generally decreases. The elbow method, silhouette, stability, downstream utility, or domain constraints can help choose k.
rationales.B: Lower or equal inertia is expected as flexibility increases.
rationales.C: The objective explicitly depends on assignments and number of centroids.
rationales.D: Increasing k can instead lead to over-fragmentation/overfitting of the geometry.
